51d5d291899f6db50e36f7114260e6ad3f1ba3d9: 1 Euro 2003 Germany incorrectly minted? "netterkerl1706" ---> What do you call this type of incorrect minting? Hello, strictly speaking, the piece shown is not a coin that was created due to an incorrect minting process. Statements from people who bring multiple stamping into play here should clearly be relegated to the realm of fantasy about stamping processes. Proof: Multiple strikes, like multiple countersinks and multiple mintings, always fundamentally require multiple contours on the coin - and these are clearly not present on this coin!! What we see during a normal and one-off embossing process are flat surrounding elevations on the pill that are embossed by a correspondingly "maltreated" embossing die. Their creation requires corresponding depressions on the embossing stamps! This coin - and almost certainly "several others" - was most likely created via a worn-out die that was "not quite properly" reconditioned for further use. This procedure of "beautifying" a stamp that is partially added, but can still be used without any problems, is the "normal case" in the mints due to economic aspects. Here, it seems that the usual use of a "mask" when cleaning an embossing die has apparently been forgotten (or it should be done quickly, right...!?). Such masks, in which only the respective coin image of a stamp is visible in the form of corresponding recesses, are intended to protect the flat stamp surface during cleaning work on the die recesses, for example when sandblasting is required. In this case, the cleaning device was used to make circular movements in the die recesses - but it appears that the device was partially or generally neglected to switch off the device briefly when moving to adjacent recesses that also needed to be cleaned (see, for example, the flat, flat-looking elevations between the eagle's head and the wing bones). Best regards varukop

ec220817ad5d9f4eee6a6968165ce3d7952a27d9: 2 x mint weakness, top 50 cents 2002 A and bottom 50 cents 2002 F. Inset Such coins were extremely rarely offered in the early 2000s and (at least in the Bay) were valued much lower, so I was able to buy them for small, double-digit euro amounts. In comparison, 2 euro coins in 2002, which only consisted of one metal, usually fetched more than 500 euros and sometimes well over 1,000 euros. 1,000 euros, which was around 3 Krugerrands back then. Today the German 2002 monometallers are often somewhere between 200 and 600 euros. And there is huge dealer inventory. Which means that 400-600 euros is still way too much. That's just a side note. End of insertion. Back to the two 50s: after new or cleaned (refurbished) stamps have been installed in the embossing machine, the embossing process begins slowly and carefully. You deliberately start with too little embossing pressure (in order to avoid defects on the stamp, ring iron and machine) and then increase it until the desired result is achieved. So if someone really wants to have the first coins minted with a new or freshly refurbished die from the regular minting process, then the coins will look like my two 50s. 2002 A is perhaps even a real "first impression" from series production (brand new stamp without peel lines) with a mirror shine that unfortunately cannot be seen in the photo. 2002 F is one of the first coins to be minted with a freshly cleaned (refurbished) die, recognizable by the embossing marks). Semi-matt and embossed without a mirror shine. The very fine dressing grooves go exactly up to the letters/numbers. This distinguishes peeling marks from rubbing marks, which do not and cast "shadows" around raised areas. The peeling marks disappear very quickly with regular stamping or are reduced very significantly, so that they are usually much less noticeable. Now you can object: “he can tell a lot here”. True. He can. If a coin was minted with far too little pressure, then the edge is round and without knurling (2002F) or (if there is a little more pressure, the knurling is only slightly present (2002A). The edge of the 50 cent coin 2002 F is pictured. Another option for skeptics: reweigh (the weights are correct, I'll save that here). Regarding the condition: for lightly minted coins, those are due to the manufacturing process Notches in the blanks are of course still present, but are a little flattened. At first glance, these look like circulation marks, but as a reminder: these are coins from regular production and not coins that were minted on pre-treated blanks (already polished before the minting process).

1c90d3cf6ed79ab7230ab8478aa0854e359d2660: @ "navada51": It depends on the type of depression and the environment of this depression. a) If you see a depression in the shape of a U-shaped "valley" on the coin, it is more likely that there was a foreign body in the minting gap. b) In scratches the “valley” is more V-shaped. c) Another important point is how close the depression reaches to the letters or other relief structures. If they stop beforehand, this is more likely to cause subsequent damage. Moin Moin, note on “navada51” - a) More likely than what? - I assume "as damage"!? With this appearance of the "U-shaped recess" ("UFV"), one should definitely not forget the possible blank error. b) I also see the sharp edge of a "V-shaped depression" ("VFV"). c) This cannot be stated in general terms. Due to its size, a foreign body can accidentally come to rest on the blank in such a way that the resulting depression ends well in front of a relief part or is partially embossed into the area of ​​the relief. A blank error can happen to be anywhere in any shape, in any place and at any conceivable distance from, for example, relief parts on the coin. Depending on its size, it is not fundamentally eliminated during embossing due to the high pressure, but is definitely reduced in size due to the material flow. Note on the questions of "coin-cidence" - 1. A certain statement can be made, as stated in a) and b), about a sharp-edged ("VFV") or rounded ("UFV") appearance, but ....... . With the "VFV" I also see more subsequent damage to the coin. With the "UFV" it is not possible to make a relatively certain statement, as it can fundamentally result from both a foreign body and a disc defect. A certain prioritization between these two options can possibly be carried out using the form of a “UFV”. - In the case of misshapen / irregular / flat "UFV", for example, there may be more evidence of a disc defect than of an imprinted foreign body. - For example, with relatively uniform / narrow / linear "UFV" the statement goes more in the direction of a foreign body that has been imprinted. 2. No. This basically depends on where the foreign body was during embossing - on the stamp or on a blank. - If it is lying loosely on the blank when minting, then in my opinion it can be assumed, as a first approximation, that it will also be transported by the minting stick when the coin is ejected. This can be embossed relatively firmly into the coin or it can remain loose. In this case, the present “misprinting” would occur once. - The production of several coins with a "UFV" (in the same place with a relatively similar appearance * ) requires that the foreign body must have remained stationary on the upper die over several minting processes. Possible, but rather unlikely in my opinion. *: not identical, but only relatively similar in appearance, as it must be assumed that the foreign body changes slightly during each embossing process due to the force applied. - One could also assume that the foreign body was on the lower stamp. Here too, in addition to the case of removal after the first embossing process (creation of unique items), several similar-looking "UFVs" could also have been created if it remained over several embossing processes. Whether they appear in the same place depends on whether the foreign body is stuck to the stamp or just loosely attached. 3. I don't see any subsequent damage to the coin presented. Based on the illustration, I tend to have a blank error.

cba30ca36b8c536dec0f8d95fcdb7c39e3b1818b: For various reasons, I did not want to have this piece discussed here in the forum, but my current level of information on this matter is so ambiguous that I would like to try to perhaps arrive at a verdict/assessment that is undoubtedly correct for me. It is the 2 cent piece below. First, my own assessment of it, chronologically: at first extremely skeptical, now uncertain and leaning towards the authenticity of the piece. The reasons for this below. The feedback I have received so far: From a forum member I highly value due to his expertise in this regard: clearly negative feedback, i.e. in the direction of manipulation - based on the images shown below. On the other hand, the verdict of a not exactly inexperienced Viennese coin dealer, who is very skeptical about such (FP) pieces, after a "live inspection": just as clearly positive feedback in the direction of a bizarre but authentic "minting accident" in connection with a double blow. Now some information about the piece, which is probably not that easy to glean from the pictures: due to the faintly visible, flattened contours on the back, the 2 cents can be clearly assigned to Austria. The forces acting on the coin (whenever and however) caused the coin to deform towards an oval. Although we are already in medias res why I now tend to consider the piece to be more authentic: very strong forces must have acted on this coin, recognizable by the flattening on the reverse (except for the crescent-shaped area near the (lower) edge) and of course also by the clear depression on the obverse (in itself a very clear sign of a double strike), which affects the largest part of it. If one assumes that there was manipulation, then there is actually only one way in which this was carried out: a 1 cent coin was placed (upside down) on top of an originally normally minted 2 cent coin and appropriately strong pressure was then applied to it (by means of a hammer blow or similar). But how can it be explained - given this "creation story" - that the details of the 2 cent embossed image were not only able to be preserved virtually undisturbed and, above all, convey the visual impression that the 2 cent embossed image was created either at the same time or after the incuse embossing with the 1 cent? Due to the rather complex topic, I would ask you to refrain from quick-fire postings in this case if possible, as they would probably not contribute anything substantial to the clarification. But I don't want to influence anyone with this: critical statements in the direction of manipulation are just as welcome as opposing ones, but I don't want to hold a majority vote on this piece, but rather (hopefully) "provoke" really well-founded statements. Oh yes, a few final information about the coin: Quality ~ excellent, "normal weight", magnetic. Alexander

This would also have to be checked for these pieces and could clarify whether this theory could be likely. 2. -------> But even with this ominous appearance, if the coins are of "normal" weight, then the nature of the materials involved must also be taken into account in all considerations - always in connection with the minting processes. I'm thinking primarily about the material flow (that one again!) - namely both metals. In order to get the transition between the pill blank and the ring to the “right” place via the material flow caused by the embossing, certain parameters must be coordinated. These include, for example, the “hardness” of the alloys that move towards one another during embossing. Basically, you have to assume that a "softer" material is superior to a "harder" one in terms of mobility, i.e. faster in a given direction (when embossing, basically radiating outwards). This means that during the embossing processes, the distances covered by the two materials are different. This is where coordination in terms of textures and, to a certain extent, but not primarily, embossing pressure come into play. The latter is always higher in the center of the embossing than in the outer areas - and there it is also raised above the minimally convex surface of the embossing die. Let's assume that for some reason during the production of the alloy mixtures, one turned out to be a little "too hard" (Cu/Ni due to an increased Ni content!?) or the other a little "too soft" (brass due to an increased Cu content!?) - or even both in combination, which would then result in the known extremes. In this case, the flow conditions of the two partners flowing toward each other automatically change during embossing. You can easily see what the later coins might look like by saying “too hard on the outside” or “too soft on the inside” or “both together”. 3. -------> Of course, an outside diameter that is too large via the embossing ring could also be involved in the possible causes or be the sole cause. This would automatically result in a lower pressure in the embossing center, which would then automatically result in a smaller flow distance of the ring material. 4. -------> Furthermore, this required flow distance could, for example, be disproportionately high and thus provide the ring material with more space to expand

719beafcd40fdd5884ed556c988d5cf0430d8ee0: The special 2 cent coin Hello Hello, today I would like to report on a great discovery in a bundle of DM miscoins that I purchased about a week ago at the coin exchange in Hanover. In addition to the incorrectly minted DM that I "coveted", this also contained five coins of the Euro currency that were insignificant to me in terms of their deviations from the norm and were also manipulated. One of the items that seemed insignificant at first glance was a 2 cent coin, which I assumed was due to a flat, narrow edge groove. However, when I fundamentally examined coins with obvious special features, the following parameters emerged that were not suitable for such a coin - and two AHA experiences: 1. Weight: 4.26 g! 2. Magnetic reaction: Yes - but relatively weak (as with three-layer materials)! 3. Color: reddish like Cu 4. Diameter: 18.75 (corresponding to 2 cents) 5. Overall appearance: Reddish colored, too thick coin with a heavily tapered circumferential groove due to the automatically increased embossing pressure/material flow and therefore only weakly pronounced. Everything about 1. to 3. speaks in favor of minting a 2 cent coin on a galvanized 2 euro pill. So it must have already accidentally ended up with the iron blanks for 2 cents at the blank manufacturers and then been further treated with them (in any case compressed and galvanized)! This galvanization also results in the weight of this coin being slightly higher than the "normal" 2 euro pills (approx. 4.10 to 4.15 g), which initially irritated me a bit. The illustrations do not say anything about the parameters 1 to 3, which are important for determining the type of misembossing, but I would still like to point them out. Best regards varukop

a1de77431f91b487c79f00906d14a0e4135296f1: Discussion: Do edge bars of different widths define variants? A wide edge bar can be explained in several ways. One of them: A used embossing stamp becomes a little jagged on the outside and is therefore turned off a bit. Then when embossing it leaves a wider edge bar than before re-twisting. Since post-processing of an embossing die cannot be ruled out as an explanation for this feature, coins that only differ from each other in the edge bar width are not per se variants. If they are to be considered variants, proof would first have to be provided that newly manufactured embossing stamps were used. The situation is different if the two coins still have differences beyond the edge bar width that can only be explained with newly made stamps.

The culprit, i.e. the one who didn't work properly here, is clearly once again the embossing pressure, which wasn't set quite harmoniously, i.e. too low. This appearance of the edge bars, which is generally possible with all coins with notches, ridges, waves, etc. created on the edges of the coin during minting, is explained by a material flow that is not completely completed during their formation due to insufficient pressure. In the appendix are a few examples, all of which got their appearance of the (partially indicated) edge bars due to insufficient embossing pressure. In addition to my labeling, the respective reason for insufficient embossing pressure is also clearly visible to the trained eye. Examples - each from left to right: >>> Incorrect setting, incorrect punching ("crescent-shaped" tooth end), "unfamiliar (oval) blank" as a result of multiple punching, incorrect setting, foreign blank, "extreme" incorrect setting (without any notches (indications), incorrect setting <<< The examples labeled incorrect setting can also be an example that is the result of a shutdown, i.e. due to a device that is no longer working optimally Minting machine but with blank feed still running unintentionally. Additional note: If you look at the two illustrations of "bremen_1", it is easy to see that the coin with the "notched" edge bars also has the less deeply pressed edge notches. This explains, for example, the many different "width" edges of the coins with notches, ridges, waves, etc., which are then referred to in the literature "slightly chamfered", "clearly chamfered", "heavily chamfered" to "not chamfered" appear. There are not, as is often assumed by the variants and stamp coupling collectors, different embossing rings "in play". Ultimately, these are only products with non-optimal embossing pressure in which the notches in the embossing ring have only been filled more or less completely through a more or less complete flow of material!!!

Hello Hello, in my opinion it is certainly not a case of manipulation, but rather the "hoped for" incorrect embossing due to a blank error, which resulted from the partial loosening by partial shearing and, after a visible change in location, the embossing of blank material again. The argument against manipulation here is the "re-embossing" (here in the base of the coin) of material that was partially sheared off in the edge bar area of ​​the blank before minting and "pushed" inwards onto the blank during shearing. This "re-imprinting" is clearly visible when looking at Fig. 3 via the visible gap between the blank and the sheared and impressed flat blank material with the dividing line in the base of the coin in front of the stars. (Some verdigris has already formed in this gap) @ Dirk Bake Your assumption about the foreign material would be theoretically conceivable if we didn't have this dividing line in the coin base that runs in front of the stars at the coin base level. In the present form, it cannot be explained by the embossing of a chip of material in the edge/edge bar area - as it cannot be caused by this. One that was coined and then fell away! A foreign object could have left a maximum of one defect in the edge corresponding to its shape. If you look at the edge there, you can also clearly see the effect of the shearing and clearly inwardly pressing edge, such as a device part (presumably and possible, for example, due to a tilting/jamming when feeding the blanks or when inserting them into the rotating multi-hole plate for feeding blanks into the embossing block). In addition, in Fig. 3 in the relevant edge bar area there is a lack of material due to the pushing away (which could not be compensated for by the embossing pressure either). too massive) material area “spared” from embossing and therefore unsmoothed. best regards varukop

2748ead3bfa27017aea21a233e93f9b2e15d7ea2: Hello and welcome here, with us "emuenzlern" in the forum. Regarding your questions: The 1 € has a very slight "decentering" and is worth keeping in mind if you are also enthusiastic about such minimal "miscoinings". However, if the decentering were a little more pronounced, it would again be very interesting, since as the number of minting years increases, the decentering becomes significantly less (in relation to the introduction of the euro in 2002), and it is also in "bfr." or "vz+". On the cent piece, such "chunks" also called "pimples" or "material surplus", there are not as common as such slight decentering on your 1 € piece, but this is not worth much more than it says on it, but the same applies here: if you like the piece, or perhaps it is even the cornerstone of a new misminting collection that you might be enthusiastic about. 32daaa9561b665d608475ab34996df72d67376a8: Hello, and welcome to the forum! 1.) Damage caused by circulation. 2.) Radiation halos occur due to wear on the stamps. The metal always flows from the inside to the outside. Therefore, over time, these stripes will eventually form that have the center point in the center. 3.) Warts, also known as pimples or metal feet, are generally not rare. These are small breaks in the die, where EVERY coin is then minted with this error. I hope this helps... But someone here obviously practiced or didn't get it right. The piece is therefore neither valuable nor collectable. Formally, “gold-plated” coins are devalued and are no longer a valid means of payment! Since they have been intentionally changed, they will no longer be exchanged by BuBa. ceafa9d3e63a5917c7ab64572c760e0b81d9ae01: Manipulation or not... @alex11: I deliberately waited a little longer before answering and took a close look at the pictures. (BEFORE I had read all the texts). Even before reading the texts, my conclusion was towards manipulation! But before I give the reasons for my decision, I would like to quickly make it clear that this cannot 100% be a double whammy (in the classic sense)! More about the reasons: 1. As Golden-Lord rightly says, the embossing pressure (also with 1c) is so great that the contours of the first embossing (undoubtedly 2c) would invariably be overembossed. 2. The Incus impression is guaranteed not to be a stamp but rather an already minted coin. Because: a) it is definitely not minted with an original die and b) the slight impressions of the edge bar of incuse 1c can also be seen in the base of the coin. 3. The coin was definitely not in a minting ring on the second strike, otherwise it would have remained round! Of course, one or more images of the edge would be all the more interesting! 4. If the piece only shows the incus impression on one side -> this means that there should have been a blind stamp on the opposite side if this really happened in the embossing machine. Therefore, in my opinion, the statement “embossing accident” in addition to the very unfortunate word “double strike” is completely inappropriate! A double strike means that the same pair of stamps hits the same blank twice! I can't say exactly why the "original impression" isn't completely covered up. Maybe there are some here who can test it by hand. However, I suspect that the back was significantly more deformed compared to the value side due to the much finer structure. Another possibility would be that the "hammer blow" was not carried out on the value side, as most people think, but on the back of the 2c. I don't really care whether the piece is untampered or not, in any case there will ALWAYS be doubts! This fact alone makes me stay away from pieces like this!

This would also have to be checked for these pieces and could clarify whether this theory could be likely. 2. -------> But even with this ominous appearance, if the coins are of "normal" weight, then the nature of the materials involved must also be taken into account in all considerations - always in connection with the minting processes. I'm thinking primarily about the material flow (that one again!) - namely both metals. In order to get the transition between the pill blank and the ring to the “right” place via the material flow caused by the embossing, certain parameters must be coordinated. These include, for example, the “hardness” of the alloys that move towards one another during embossing. Basically, you have to assume that a "softer" material is superior to a "harder" one in terms of mobility, i.e. faster in a given direction (when embossing, basically radiating outwards). This means that during the embossing processes, the distances covered by the two materials are different. This is where coordination in terms of textures and, to a certain extent, but not primarily, embossing pressure come into play. The latter is always higher in the center of the embossing than in the outer areas - and there it is also raised above the minimally convex surface of the embossing die. Let's assume that for some reason during the production of the alloy mixtures, one turned out to be a little "too hard" (Cu/Ni due to an increased Ni content!?) or the other a little "too soft" (brass due to an increased Cu content!?) - or even both in combination, which would then result in the known extremes. In this case, the flow conditions of the two partners flowing toward each other automatically change during embossing. You can easily see what the later coins might look like by saying “too hard on the outside” or “too soft on the inside” or “both together”. 3. -------> Of course, an outside diameter that is too large via the embossing ring could also be involved in the possible causes or be the sole cause. This would automatically result in a lower pressure in the embossing center, which would then automatically result in a smaller flow distance of the ring material. 4. -------> Furthermore, this required flow distance could be influenced, for example, by edge bar heights and/or widths that are disproportionate and thus provide the ring material with more space to expand. The pressure resulting from inward flow would decrease, thereby also shortening the flow distance of this material. The result would be a pill with a larger diameter, which would then automatically protrude beyond the desired (material) meeting point. 5. -------> The various possible combinations of the possible reasons listed should not be forgotten either. 6. -------> After sending it, I just saw that "navada51" got ahead of me a little while I was writing about the possibilities of reasons for the hardships. 7c4a23ea0695942b958418b0d1d3503ab1aa418a: Hello Hello, this one-sided, narrow excess of material on the outside on approx. 1 third to half of the edge bar *, which is associated with the "off-center" embossing described in #3479, occurs when one of the stamps is not firmly positioned (or perhaps installed incorrectly) and does not meet the blank completely flat during the embossing. This tilting creates a minimal gap in part of the outer area during the embossing process between the corresponding embossing die and the embossing ring, into which blank material automatically flows due to the high embossing pressure, thus causing the visible outer edge bar increase. In the present case it is the type of misprinting "one-sided decentering" - here, however, a minimal one and generally very common and certainly not "the discovery of the century". Note: Very sharp-edged elevations on the outside of the entire edge bar can often be noticed even on machines that are working properly when using the "PP" manufacturing process due to the significantly higher embossing pressure required compared to normal embossing. * not edge, because that is the coin area with the edge waves

095f6fc05fc150db307f01293f6e4baa2ad0daed: Hello, welcome to the forum! This type of incorrect minting occurs quite frequently with all denominations. These are embossings that were "only partially made in the embossing ring" because the blank was not correctly inserted into the embossing ring. The edge designs in the form of "smooth", "Spanish rose" (only the edge dents!), "notches" ("ripples") and "waves" are created when embossing using the embossing ring into which these features are incorporated. The "Spanish Rose" represents a special case, because the part of it that is visible on the value and back is created using the two embossing stamps in which it is incorporated. When embossing, this requires firstly a very precise adjustment of the two embossing stamps to each other and secondly to the embossing ring. Only with the correct installation of these three tools involved in the embossing and their correct interaction can the "Spanish Rose" be created as a continuous decoration from the value side to the back.

Decentering and minting weakness is a bit much for a single coin if it is genuine. In order to be able to say something more, you would need better (sharper) pictures, less background, fewer megabytes, indication of weight to the nearest 2 decimal places, reaction to a magnet (please test the ring and pill separately), a precise description and if possible a good picture of the edge embossing (it should be grooved and the text "UNITY AND LAW AND FREEDOM" should be read, the beginning/end of which is marked by an eagle. With counterfeits you often have extremely strong reactions to them Magnets, or no reaction at all, or a reaction that is as weak as with real pieces, because the counterfeiters now incorporate pieces of iron into the pill. The edge embossing usually has errors: 1. the fluting is often too weak or irregular. 2. the text is often not entirely correct (Hs are sometimes confused with Ms and then it says "UNITY AND RECMT AND FREEDOM"). On top of that, instead of a federal eagle, there is usually just a diamond embossed. A decent one A picture of the value side would also be helpful. It is best not to simply take the pictures with your cell phone and upload them directly, but to crop them on the PC before uploading them and shrink them to a size that you can view them on a 17'' notebook monitor without it bursting. If you can't see anything, the picture is simply not sharp enough.

Hello, strictly speaking, the piece shown is not a coin that was created due to an incorrect minting process. Statements from people who bring multiple stamping into play here should clearly be relegated to the realm of fantasy about stamping processes. Proof: Multiple strikes, like multiple countersinks and multiple mintings, always fundamentally require multiple contours on the coin - and these are clearly not present on this coin!! What we see during a normal and one-off embossing process are flat surrounding elevations on the pill that are embossed by a correspondingly "maltreated" embossing die. Their creation requires corresponding depressions on the embossing stamps! This coin - and almost certainly "several others" - was most likely created via a worn-out die that was "not quite properly" reconditioned for further use. This procedure of "beautifying" a stamp that is partially added, but can still be used without any problems, is the "normal case" in the mints due to economic aspects. Here, it seems that the usual use of a "mask" when cleaning an embossing die has apparently been forgotten (or it should be done quickly, right...!?). Such masks, in which only the respective coin image of a stamp is visible in the form of corresponding recesses, are intended to protect the flat stamp surface during cleaning work on the die recesses, for example when sandblasting is required. "netterkerl1706" ---> What do you call this type of incorrect minting? Hello, strictly speaking, the piece shown is not a coin that was created due to an incorrect minting process. Statements from people who bring multiple stamping into play here should clearly be relegated to the realm of fantasy about stamping processes. Proof: Multiple strikes, like multiple countersinks and multiple mintings, always fundamentally require multiple contours on the coin - and these are clearly not present on this coin!! What we see during a normal and one-off embossing process are flat surrounding elevations on the pill that are embossed by a correspondingly "maltreated" embossing die. Their creation requires corresponding depressions on the embossing stamps! This coin - and almost certainly "several others" - was most likely created via a worn-out die that was "not quite properly" reconditioned for further use. This procedure of "beautifying" a stamp that is partially added, but can still be used without any problems, is the "normal case" in the mints due to economic aspects. (BEFORE I had read all the texts). Even before reading the texts, my conclusion was towards manipulation! But before I give the reasons for my decision, I would like to quickly make it clear that this cannot 100% be a double whammy (in the classic sense)! More about the reasons: 1. As Golden-Lord rightly says, the embossing pressure (also with 1c) is so great that the contours of the first embossing (undoubtedly 2c) would invariably be overembossed. 2. The Incus impression is guaranteed not to be a stamp but rather an already minted coin. Because: a) it is definitely not minted with an original die and b) the slight impressions of the edge bar of incuse 1c can also be seen in the base of the coin. 3. The coin was definitely not in a minting ring on the second strike, otherwise it would have remained round! Of course, one or more images of the edge would be all the more interesting! 4. If the piece only shows the incus impression on one side -> this means that there should have been a blind stamp on the opposite side if this really happened in the embossing machine. Therefore, in my opinion, the statement “embossing accident” in addition to the very unfortunate word “double strike” is completely inappropriate! A double strike means that the same pair of stamps hits the same blank twice! I can't say exactly why the "original impression" isn't completely covered up. Maybe there are some here who can test it by hand. However, I suspect that the back was significantly more deformed compared to the value side due to the much finer structure. Another possibility would be that the "hammer blow" was not carried out on the value side, as most people think, but on the back of the 2c. I don't really care whether the piece is untampered or not, in any case there will ALWAYS be doubts! This fact alone makes me stay away from pieces like this!

One of them: A used embossing stamp becomes a little jagged on the outside and is therefore turned off a bit. Then when embossing it leaves a wider edge bar than before re-twisting. Since post-processing of an embossing die cannot be ruled out as an explanation for this feature, coins that only differ from each other in the edge bar width are not per se variants. If they are to be considered variants, proof would first have to be provided that newly manufactured embossing stamps were used. The situation is different if the two coins still have differences beyond the edge bar width that can only be explained with newly made stamps.
